course_details.Overview of class: This core course focuses on what it means to be - or what it meant to be - a musician at different times in history and in different cultural contexts, with a specific focus on our own performance lineages as versatile, yet mostly classical, musicians in 21st-century America. It will explore different types of musical performances, the careers and obstacles faced by specific performers throughout history, look at the roles of contrasting performance venues, and analyze what makes some artists and some performances successful. Case studies presented during the class include the history of conductors, classical music in East Asia, jazz pianists and singers, issues of gender and race in opera, Black musicians in twentieth-century America, and the history of wind bands, among others. By these means, music students will gain introductory literacy in diverse types of performance practices, learn about the legacies of important musicians, and better understand intersections between creativity and commerce in music fields. Among individual projects will be an investigation of the history of performance in each student's specific major, including their lineage of teachers, and a critical analysis of different performance modes.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
• Learn about musicians, their legacies, and the circumstances of their performances in varied global and local contexts
• Conceive of music history through the lens of performers rather than through the composer or the work
• Develop a sense of how the concept of a work differs from the concept of performance, and engage, where applicable, with notions of performance practices
• Experience different types of musical performances and critically engage with them
• Historicize and locate yourself within a complex landscape of musicians, past and present
course_details.Class Materials (Required): No required textbook purchases. Students will be expected to attend live performances of their choice, some of which may charge admission.

course_details.Learning Objectives: Level 5 is a sequel to Level 4 and provides students of intermediate level with a wide range of keyboard skills emphasizing SATB chorale score reading, accompanying and collaborative skills, and advanced keyboard theory. Other keyboard theory topics include Augmented sixth chords, Neapolitan-sixth chords. Continuing skills are two-hand creative accompaniments from existing harmonizations, and solo repertoire, and technique. Students will also reinforce and apply the theory concepts learned through the quarter in a composition project. The solo piano Quarter-Long Piece will emphasize musical expression and cumulative reading skills in the setting of a class recital.

course_details.Overview of class: As an introduction to the basic tools of resources in music research, the class includes study of general library resources, bibliographies of composers, music, music literature, and music sources. Students will experience a broad view of music reference tools and editions of music. Key projects in the class are providing an appropriate bibliography for a selected research topic and selecting an appropriate performing edition for practical use based on a variety of sources.
course_details.Learning Objectives:
Through class discussion, readings and assignments, students will:
• Become familiar with basic music research resources; develop expertise in using standard tools
• Learn to evaluate information resources
• Develop an understanding of the research process including citation style/management
• Use music repertoire guides to identify musical literature
• Develop expertise needed to evaluate variant editions of musical works
• Learn a basic understanding of copyright and intellectual property law and practice
course_details.Evaluation Method: Weekly assignments and one term length project. There is no final.
